source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN Examination, 7th ed.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client returns from microvascular decompression of the trigeminal nerve. Which equipment should the nurse ask the aide to place at the bedside?
questions.rationale: Care is the same as after craniotomy: hourly neurologic checks (pupils with a flashlight) and monitoring of cardiovascular and respiratory status (pulse oximetry).
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1170 (PDF p. 1457)
questions.quote: This client requires hourly neurological assessment as well as monitoring of the cardiovascular and respiratory statuses.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with Guillain-Barré syndrome has paralysis ascending to the waist. Which equipment should be ready for emergencies?
questions.rationale: Ascending paralysis can cause respiratory failure, so an intubation tray is kept ready. Cardiac dysrhythmias also occur, so cardiac monitoring is needed.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1171 (PDF p. 1458)
questions.quote: The client with Guillain-Barré syndrome is at risk for respiratory failure as a result of ascending paralysis.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A stroke client coughs when swallowing and now has a temperature of 38.3°C, SpO2 of 91%, confusion, and dyspnea. What should the nurse do?
questions.rationale: These are signs of aspiration (fever, dyspnea, low oxygen, confusion). A complication has developed, so the provider is notified.
explanations: Too late as the only action.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1198 (PDF p. 1490)
questions.quote: The client is exhibiting clinical signs and symptoms of aspiration, which include fever, dyspnea, decreased arterial oxygen levels, and confusion.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.situation: Mang Tomas, 52, is admitted with a leaking cerebral aneurysm and is scheduled for surgery.
questions.stem: Which intervention should the nurse implement before surgery?
questions.rationale: Aneurysm precautions keep activity minimal to prevent straining (Valsalva), which raises blood pressure and increases bleeding.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1206 (PDF p. 1498)
questions.quote: the client’s activity is kept to a minimum to prevent Valsalva’s maneuver.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.situation: Mang Tomas, 52, is admitted with a leaking cerebral aneurysm and is scheduled for surgery.
questions.stem: Mang Tomas's daughter asks to take him to the lounge 'for just a few minutes.' What should the nurse explain?
questions.rationale: Aneurysm precautions minimize stimuli that could raise intracranial pressure and trigger bleeding or rupture. Reduced stimuli do not speed healing.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1543 (PDF p. 1855)
questions.quote: Subarachnoid precautions (or aneurysm precautions) are intended to minimize environmental stimuli, which could increase intracranial pressure

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.situation: Mang Tomas, 52, is admitted with a leaking cerebral aneurysm and is scheduled for surgery.
questions.stem: Which medication order should the nurse QUESTION for a client with a ruptured intracranial aneurysm?
questions.rationale: Heparin, an anticoagulant, raises the risk of rebleeding. Nicardipine manages vasospasm, docusate prevents straining, and aminocaproic acid prevents clot breakdown.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1463 (PDF p. 1772)
questions.quote: The nurse should question a prescription for heparin sodium, which is an anticoagulant.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with Bell's palsy is upset about her face. What should the nurse tell her?
options: It often resolves in 3 to 5 weeks
questions.rationale: Clients are reassured that it is not a stroke and that symptoms often disappear on their own in about 3 to 5 weeks. Treatment is supportive.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1408 (PDF p. 1714)
questions.quote: symptoms often disappear spontaneously in approximately 3 to 5 weeks.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which finding is the PRIMARY indicator of neurologic status in a client with an acute head injury?
questions.rationale: LOC is the primary indicator. It changes before other neurologic signs or vital signs.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1445 (PDF p. 1754)
questions.quote: The level of consciousness is the primary indicator of neurological status.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: During a seizure, a client's whole body becomes rigid, then all four limbs alternately contract and relax. How should the nurse document this?
questions.rationale: Tonic-clonic seizures begin with rigidity (tonic) followed by rhythmic contraction and relaxation (clonic). Absence seizures are brief lapses with a blank stare.
explanations: Brief lapse with a blank stare.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1450 (PDF p. 1759)
questions.quote: Tonic-clonic seizures are characterized by body rigidity (tonic phase) followed by rhythmic jerky contraction and relaxation of all body muscles

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: A client with a right-sided stroke has left-sided neglect. Which action would REINFORCE the neglect?
options: Teach him to scan to the left
Keep his items on the right side only
Place the chair on his left
Touch his left arm when talking
questions.rationale: The nurse refocuses the client's attention to the affected side. Items, the chair, and the commode are placed on the affected side, and the client is taught to scan toward it.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1451 (PDF p. 1760)
questions.quote: The nurse’s role is to refocus the client’s attention to the affected side.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: When would continued fatigue suggest a client's myasthenia gravis drugs are not optimal?
questions.rationale: In myasthenia gravis, weakness appears after exertion and near the end of the day. If fatigue persists then despite therapy, the regimen may need adjusting.
explanations: Correct: the typical timing of weakness.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1452 (PDF p. 1761)
questions.quote: The client with myasthenia gravis has weakness after periods of exertion and near the end of the day.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which symptom does the nurse expect in a client with trigeminal neuralgia?
options: Sudden pain along cranial nerve V
questions.rationale: Trigeminal neuralgia is abrupt-onset pain involving one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V).
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1497 (PDF p. 1806)
questions.quote: It involves one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V).

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which can trigger the pain of trigeminal neuralgia?
questions.rationale: Stimulating trigeminal nerve branches triggers pain: washing the face, brushing teeth, shaving, eating, yawning, or temperature stimuli such as a draft.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1527 (PDF p. 1837)
questions.quote: Symptoms can be triggered by pressure from washing the face, brushing the teeth, shaving, eating and drinking, and yawning.

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: Which findings does the nurse expect in a client with Bell's palsy?
options: One-sided facial droop and trouble chewing
questions.rationale: Bell's palsy is one-sided facial paralysis from compression of cranial nerve VII. It causes facial droop, increased tearing, pain near the ear, and difficulty chewing.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1528 (PDF p. 1838)
questions.quote: Bell’s palsy is a one-sided facial paralysis resulting from compression of the facial nerve (CN VII).

questions.subject: NP IV
questions.stem: When taking the history of a client with Guillain-Barré syndrome, the nurse should ask about a recent:
questions.rationale: Many clients report a respiratory or GI infection 1 to 4 weeks before the onset of neurologic deficits.
questions.source: Saunders Q&A Review for the NCLEX-RN, 7th ed., Q1531 (PDF p. 1841)
questions.quote: Many clients report a history of respiratory or GI infection in the 1 to 4 weeks before the onset of neurological deficits.
